wine.name: Château Lafite Rothschild
wine.classification: Premier Cru Classé in the 1855 classification of the Médoc
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the great majority, with Merlot and small parts of Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot.
wine.sites: Deep gravel slopes in the north of Pauillac, running to the border with Saint-Estèphe, and the Carruades plateau beside them.
wine.making: Fermented in vats for about a fortnight at a controlled temperature. Each barrel is then tasted on its own before the blend is made, and the wine is aged in new oak barrels for about fifteen months, by the estate's own account, before it is bottled at the château.
wine.glass: Cedar, pencil shavings and cassis over violet and graphite, more perfume than power, with fine, firm tannin, fresh acidity and a long, dry finish of cigar box.
wine.ageing: Closed for its first ten to fifteen years in a strong vintage, it can then hold and develop for half a century.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, and an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The commune appellation, red wine only, between Saint-Julien and Saint-Estèphe.
Bottled at the estate rather than by a merchant in Bordeaux.
The family name the estate took after Baron James de Rothschild bought it in 1868.

records.table: Château Lafite Rothschild stands first in the 1855 list of the Médoc's first growths: Pauillac, mostly Cabernet Sauvignon, from gravel by the Saint-Estèphe border. Expect cedar, pencil shavings and cassis, more perfume than power, built to age for decades.
records.story: Vines were planted at Lafite in the late seventeenth century by the Ségur family, as the estate tells it, and in the eighteenth century Nicolas-Alexandre de Ségur (1697 to 1755), who also held Latour, was remembered as the Prince of the Vines. The story goes that the military governor of Guyenne, a friend of the king, made Lafite the wine of the court at Versailles. Heavy debts forced a later Ségur to sell in 1784, to a kinsman who was guillotined in 1794, and the estate was seized and sold as national property. When the Bordeaux brokers drew up their classification for the Universal Exhibition in Paris in 1855, Lafite stood first among the four first growths. On 8 August 1868 Baron James de Rothschild (1792 to 1868), head of the family's Paris bank, bought it at auction in Paris, against a coalition of Bordeaux merchants, in the estate's version of the sale, and he died that November, three months later. The estate took the family's name, and the label as it is known first appeared on the next vintage. The Carruades plateau that adjoins the vineyard gives its name to the second wine. Lafite is the perfumed, restrained side of Pauillac, the first growth that whispers rather than shouts.

others.name: Carruades de Lafite
others.note: The second wine, named for the Carruades plateau, a group of plots that adjoins the ridge of the grand vin's vineyard.

traps: Carruades de Lafite is the second wine, not the grand vin.
Lafite is in Pauillac, not Saint-Estèphe, though its vines run to the border.
Lafite and Mouton were bought by different branches of the Rothschild family, Mouton in 1853 and Lafite in 1868.

cards.front: Château Lafite Rothschild: who bought it in 1868, and what happened next?
cards.back: Baron James de Rothschild (1792 to 1868) of the Paris bank, at auction; he died three months later and the estate took the family's name.

cards.front: Which grape leads Château Lafite Rothschild, and what is its second wine?
cards.back: Cabernet Sauvignon, the great majority; the second wine is Carruades de Lafite.

questions.q: A guest wants the second wine of Château Lafite Rothschild. Which bottle do you bring?
questions.exp: Carruades de Lafite, named for a plateau beside the vineyard, is Lafite's second wine; Les Forts is Latour's, Pavillon Rouge is Margaux's and Le Petit Mouton is Mouton's.

questions.exp: He bought Lafite on 8 August 1868 and died that November; Brane-Mouton had been bought by Nathaniel de Rothschild in 1853 and renamed Mouton.

wine.name: Château Latour
wine.classification: Premier Cru Classé in the 1855 classification of the Médoc
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, by far the larger part, with Merlot and touches of Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot.
wine.sites: L'Enclos, the walled heart of the estate on deep gravel above the Gironde at the southern edge of Pauillac, by the Saint-Julien border; fruit from outside it goes to the second and third wines.
wine.making: Fermented in temperature controlled stainless steel vats, first installed in 1964, and aged for eighteen months or more in new oak barrels before bottling at the château; the wines are then held at the estate until it judges them ready.
wine.glass: Cassis, blackberry and cigar box over graphite and an iron, almost bloody note; dense and grippy, with high, firm tannin, fresh acidity and a long, tight finish.
wine.ageing: Austere for fifteen to twenty years in a strong vintage, it then lasts for decades, and it holds its shape even in weak years.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for two hours or more, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The first wine, as the label prints it, drawn from L'Enclos.
The commune appellation, red wine only, between Saint-Julien and Saint-Estèphe.
Bottled at the estate rather than by a merchant in Bordeaux.

records.table: Château Latour is the Pauillac first growth named for the tower that guarded the Gironde in the Hundred Years War. Mostly Cabernet Sauvignon from the walled Enclos, it is dense and firm and needs decades, so decant it well.
records.story: A fortified tower stood here in the fourteenth century, guarding the estuary during the Hundred Years War, and it gave the estate its name; the round tower shown on every label was built later, in the seventeenth century. By the early eighteenth century Latour had joined Lafite in the hands of the Ségur family, and in 1855 the Bordeaux brokers ranked it among the four first growths. The Ségur heirs kept it until 1963, when they sold a majority to the British Pearson group, with Harveys of Bristol beside it. The new owners modernised the cellar and in 1964 replaced the old wooden vats with temperature controlled stainless steel, three years after Haut-Brion. Les Forts de Latour, the second wine, followed with the 1966 vintage, and the estate returned to French hands in 1993. Latour is famous for consistency: its deep gravel by the river gives a wine that holds its shape in weak years, and its 1961 is a vintage of history. With the 2012 vintage it left the en primeur system, the sale of wine still in barrel, and has since released its wines when it judges them ready to drink.

others.name: Les Forts de Latour
others.note: The second wine in its modern form, from the 1966 vintage, mostly from parcels outside L'Enclos.

others.name: Pauillac de Latour
others.note: The third wine, labelled simply by its commune.

Château Latour in Pauillac is a different estate from Latour-Martillac in Pessac-Léognan and La Tour Carnet in the Haut-Médoc.
Latour left the en primeur system with the 2012 vintage, so its wines reach the market only when the estate releases them.

cards.back: The walled heart of the estate on deep gravel above the Gironde; it gives the grand vin, while other parcels go to the second and third wines.

cards.front: What did Château Latour change in its cellar in 1964?

questions.q: A guest asks why Château Latour is known for holding up even in weak vintages. Which reason fits?

A high share of Merlot on cool clay

questions.exp: L'Enclos lies on deep, warm gravel beside the estuary, which drains well and ripens Cabernet Sauvignon even in hard years; the blend is mostly Cabernet, not Merlot.

wine.name: Château Margaux
wine.classification: Premier Cru Classé in the 1855 classification of the Médoc
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the larger part, with Merlot and a little Petit Verdot and Cabernet Franc.
wine.sites: Gravel croupes, low rises of deep gravel, in the commune of Margaux around the château; a separate parcel of Sauvignon Blanc gives the white.
wine.making: Fermented in vats, then racked off its lees after the malolactic and put into new French oak barrels in late October or November. It ages there for eighteen months to two years, about twenty-one months on average, on an estate that keeps its own cooperage beside the cellars, before bottling at the château.
wine.glass: Violet, rose petal and cassis over cedar and cool graphite, with blackberry and a little liquorice; fine grained, silky tannin, bright acidity and a long, lifted finish.
wine.ageing: Charming earlier than Latour, it still needs ten to fifteen years in a strong vintage and can last half a century.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The words the estate uses for its first growth rank of 1855.
Both the estate and the commune appellation, red only; the estate's white is sold as Bordeaux.
Bottled at the estate rather than by a merchant in Bordeaux.

records.table: Château Margaux is the first growth of the Margaux appellation, a Cabernet Sauvignon led wine of violets, cassis and silk, made behind a neoclassical château of the 1810s. Its white, Pavillon Blanc, is sold as plain Bordeaux.
records.story: In the 1570s the Lestonnac family reshaped the old domain at Margaux around its vineyards, as the estate tells it. In 1787 Thomas Jefferson (1743 to 1826), then the American minister in Paris, toured Bordeaux and named Château Margaux among four wines of the first quality, with Latour, Haut-Brion and Lafite. After the Revolution the estate was sold as national property, and its new owner of 1801 had a Bordeaux architect build the neoclassical château, begun in 1810, whose front appears on the label. In 1855 the brokers ranked Château Margaux a first growth, one of only four reds. The twentieth century was harder: the Ginestet family, who had come to own the whole estate by about 1950, were left in difficulty by the slump of the 1970s and sold it in 1977 to André Mentzelopoulos (1915 to 1980). He drained and replanted the vineyard, with the oenologist Émile Peynaud (1912 to 2004) as adviser, and by his death in 1980 the estate was held to have its old standing back. Its white, Pavillon Blanc, is all Sauvignon Blanc, and since the Margaux appellation is for red wine alone it must be sold as Bordeaux Blanc.

wine.name: Château Haut-Brion
wine.classification: Premier Cru Classé in 1855, and a Cru Classé de Graves for its red in 1959
wine.grapes: Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon, the lead passing between them with the year, with Cabernet Franc for the rest.
wine.sites: Gravel mounds in Pessac around the château, long since surrounded by the suburbs of Bordeaux.
wine.making: Fermented in stainless steel vats, first installed in 1961, the first of the first growths to use them, then aged for eighteen to twenty months in oak barrels, the share of new oak set each year by the vintage, before bottling at the château.
wine.glass: Tobacco leaf, cigar box and wood smoke over cassis and ripe black cherry, with warm gravel, a little truffle and fine, sweet tannin; savoury, supple and long.
wine.ageing: Open sooner than the Pauillac first growths, it still rewards fifteen years and can last for more than half a century.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The appellation of the northern Graves, created in 1987, where Haut-Brion lies.
The older name of the district, printed on bottles from before Pessac-Léognan was carved out of it.

records.table: Château Haut-Brion is the one first growth of 1855 outside the Médoc, from gravel in Pessac long since surrounded by the suburbs of Bordeaux. Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon give tobacco, wood smoke and cassis, more savoury than the Pauillacs.
records.story: In 1525 a marriage brought part of the Haut-Brion land to the Pontac family as a bride's dowry; in 1533 the bridegroom bought its manorial rights from a Basque merchant, and in 1549 he began the château. By the 1660s the wine was known in London by the estate's own name: on 10 April 1663 Samuel Pepys (1633 to 1703) wrote in his diary of drinking, at the Royal Oak tavern in Lombard Street, a French wine called Ho Bryan, and in 1666 the family opened a London tavern of its own, Pontack's Head. Thomas Jefferson (1743 to 1826) came on 25 May 1787 and bought its wine, and the statesman Talleyrand (1754 to 1838) owned it briefly in the early nineteenth century. In 1855 the brokers ranked it a first growth beside three Médoc estates, though it lies in the Graves. In 1935 a New York banker bought it, and the second wine, Le Clarence, carries his first name. In 1959 it was classified again, among the red Crus Classés de Graves, and in 1961 it became the first of the first growths to ferment in stainless steel vats. The white, Haut-Brion Blanc, carries no classification of its own.

wine.name: Château Mouton Rothschild
wine.classification: Premier Cru Classé since 1973; a second growth in the 1855 classification
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the great majority, with Merlot and small parts of Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot.
wine.sites: The Mouton plateau of deep gravel in the north of Pauillac, beside Lafite.
wine.making: Fermented parcel by parcel, mostly in oak vats with some of steel, in a vat room fed by gravity, then aged for about twenty months in new oak barrels before bottling at the château, where the whole crop has been bottled since the 1924 vintage.
wine.glass: Cassis, blackcurrant leaf and mint over cigar box, roasted coffee and sweet cedar; opulent and dense, with firm, ripe tannin, fresh acidity and a long finish of clove and graphite.
wine.ageing: Opulent enough to tempt early, it needs fifteen years in a strong vintage and can last for decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for two hours, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Since 1945 a different artist has made the work at the head of each year's label.
The commune appellation, red wine only, between Saint-Julien and Saint-Estèphe.
Bottled at the estate, which Mouton did with its whole crop from 1924.

records.table: Château Mouton Rothschild is the Pauillac first growth that had to fight for its rank: promoted in 1973, the one promotion in the 1855 list. Cabernet Sauvignon gives cassis, cigar box and coffee, and every vintage since 1945 carries an artist's label.
records.story: First I cannot be, second I do not deign, Mouton I am: so ran the old motto of an estate that Baron Nathaniel de Rothschild (1812 to 1870), of the English branch of the family, bought in 1853, when it was Château Brane-Mouton, and that then took the family's name. Two years later the brokers' classification of 1855 placed it among the second growths, a rank the family would not accept. His great grandson, Baron Philippe de Rothschild (1902 to 1988), took charge in 1922, barely twenty, and from the 1924 vintage bottled the whole crop at the château, where until then the wine had been sold in barrel to the Bordeaux merchants; that year's label was drawn by a young poster artist in the Cubist manner. In 1945 he marked the year of victory with a label bearing a V for victory, by a then unknown illustrator, and since then a different artist has made the work at the head of each year's label. After some twenty years of campaigning, a decree of 1973 made Mouton a first growth, and the motto became: first I am, second I was, Mouton does not change. In 1978 Philippe de Rothschild agreed with a Napa winemaker to make one wine together, Opus One, first made from the 1979 vintage.

traps: The 1973 promotion is the one change of rank in the 1855 red list; no estate has been demoted.
Mouton Cadet is a merchant's brand from the same family, not the estate's second wine.
Mouton was bought in 1853 by the English branch of the Rothschilds; Lafite came to the French branch in 1868.

cards.front: Château Mouton Rothschild: what changed in 1973?
cards.back: A decree promoted it from second growth to first growth, the one promotion in the 1855 list, and its motto changed to first I am, second I was, Mouton does not change.

cards.front: What has Château Mouton Rothschild's label carried each year since 1945?
cards.back: A work by a different artist, a series begun with the V for victory label marking 1945, the year of victory.

questions.q: A guest at a Bordeaux dinner wants the dry white made at Château Mouton Rothschild. Which wine is it?
questions.exp: Aile d'Argent is the estate's dry white, sold as Bordeaux Blanc; Pavillon Blanc is Margaux's, Le Petit Mouton is the second red, and Mouton Cadet is a merchant's brand.

questions.q: In which year was Château Mouton Rothschild promoted from second growth to first growth by decree?
questions.exp: A decree of 1973 made Mouton a first growth, the one promotion in the 1855 list; 1924 was its first whole château bottling and 1945 the first label of the artist series.
